newsitem.title: USA: Nepal economy robust, but reforms needed--IMF.
newsitem.headline: Nepal economy robust, but reforms needed--IMF.

text.p: Nepal's economy remains robust and its inflation under control, but the country needs tax reform, tight monetary policy and faster privatization to ensure continuing growth, the International Monetary Fund said on Friday.
In its latest Article IV report on Nepal, completed May 28 and released on Friday, the IMF also expressed concerns over the country's fiscal and current account deficits.
"Directors supported the authorities' goal to raise domestic savings ... especially in view of Nepal's large current account deficit," the report stated.

The IMF added that the government should move ahead with plans to introduce a value-added tax in 1997, and should enact measures to "broaden the tax base" by reducing tax holidays and specific tax exemptions.
IMF directors advised that "monetary policy would need to remain tight to safeguard the buildup in international reserves and to keep inflation low."

Banking system strains resulting from financial problems at Nepal's state-owned and largest bank, the Rastriya Banijya Bank, highlight the need to restructure and ultimately privatize the bank, the report stated.
"The privatization program should be strengthened, and ... control and ownership in the telecommunications, transportation and financial sectors should be shifted to private hands," the IMF said.
Directors generally supported Nepal's fixed exchange rate peg with India, which the report said had fostered financial discipline and regional economic integration.
But given India's moves toward liberalization and capital account convertibility, the directors recommended that Nepal revisit the issue of the peg over time.
The IMF estimated Nepal in its 1996/97 fiscal year, which ends on July 15, posted gross domestic product growth of 4.9 percent, with inflation between eight and nine percent.
Nepal will also post a current account deficit of 10.6 percent of GDP and a fiscal shortfall of 3.8 percent of GDP, IMF estimated.
